source: Cook, Goodman & Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play (Cognition 120:341)
finding: The founding developmental EIG paper. Authors write EIg(A)=sum_i P(D_i|A) Ig(D_i,A), where Ig is the drop in Shannon uncertainty over hypotheses. They argue the prior P(H) and knowledge of affordances P(D|A,H) both enter the score. Prediction: children isolate variables only when evidence is ambiguous.
numbers: Formal setup: 4 objects of uncertain causal status, 3 possible actions (two test one bead each, one tests a stuck pair together = confounded). Mean age 54 months.
quote: Probabilistic models of expected information gain require integrating prior knowledge about causal hypotheses with knowledge about possible actions
limits: Authors do not claim children know experimental design principles, only that behaviour is selective. Lab task has a tiny, hand-built action set.
agent_relevance: A scaffold step should rank candidate probes by expected drop in uncertainty over hypotheses, using both current beliefs and what each probe can actually isolate.

source: Cook et al. (2011) Experiment 1 (same paper)
finding: 60 preschoolers saw a machine that lights up. All Beads: every training bead worked (little to learn). Some Beads (B or AB): only half worked (ambiguous). Then a stuck pair and a separable pair were shown, 60 s free play. Informative experiment = pull the separable pair apart and test each bead alone.
numbers: All Beads: 1 of 20 children (5%) did it; 65% never pulled the pair apart. Some Beads B: 9/20 (45%). Some Beads AB: 10/20 (50%). Vs All Beads: chi2(1,N=40)=8.53 and 10.16, both p<.005. Some Beads B vs AB: chi2=0.10 ns.
limits: Conservative criterion (both beads tested alone). Warm-up play time (about 29-33 s) and number of play categories (3.83, 4.06, 3.95; F(2,60)=1.08 ns) did not differ, so it was not just more varied play. Only 45-50% did it even when it paid.
agent_relevance: Probe choice depends on ambiguity: when beliefs are settled the probe is skipped. An agent should skip probing when the posterior is already sharp.

source: Cook et al. (2011) Experiment 2 (same paper)
finding: 40 preschoolers saw only the stuck pair. The informative action had to be invented: orient the pair vertically so one end touches at a time. It was never demonstrated.
numbers: Some Beads: 9/20 (45%) did it (3 saw only the second bead work, 6 saw both); All Beads: 1/20 (5%). chi2(1,N=40)=8.53, p<.005. Mean play categories 3.00 vs 2.78, t(40)=0.89 ns. 5 children replaced. Intercoder agreement 86% (kappa .71).
limits: Small N per cell; 55% of children in the ambiguous condition still did not do it. Authors say the intervention was non-obvious even to them. Children were wrong about the mechanism (anything pressing the platform worked), so this shows probe design, not correct causal knowledge.
agent_relevance: Probe invention (not only choice from a menu) is within reach of young learners; for an agent, let the model propose probes and let code score them.

source: Cook et al. (2011) discussion of limits (same paper)
finding: Authors state the study does not show children understand why isolating variables works, and that formal control of variables needs explicit awareness. Exploratory play serves many aims besides information.
numbers: No extra numbers.
limits: Authors list sensorimotor stimulation, skill learning and temperament as other drivers of play.
agent_relevance: Do not treat EIG as the only drive; keep task value separate from information value in the scaffold.

source: Coenen, Nelson & Gureckis (2019) Asking the right questions about the psychology of human inquiry: Nine open challenges (Psychon Bull Rev 26:1548)
finding: Review of optimal experiment design (OED) as a model of human inquiry. Expected usefulness of a query = sum over answers P(a|Q) U(a), with U = Shannon entropy drop (EIG), KL divergence, probability gain or error reduction. EIG and KL give the same expected value for every question but can disagree on single answers.
numbers: Table 2 gives six belief-change scenarios where IG, KL and probability gain disagree. Cited uses: Oaksford & Chater 1994 (cards), Steyvers et al. 2003 (causal networks), Najemnik & Geisler 2005 (eye movements), Nelson et al. 2014.
quote: The question of how to apply OED principles to more open-ended natural language question asking exposes more than just the issue of how this large space can be searched.
limits: Authors argue OED has blind spots: it assumes hypothesis and answer sets are known, ignores cost and motivation, and assumes ideal belief updating.
agent_relevance: Pick one scoring rule and state it; EIG and probability gain can rank probes differently, so test both against outcomes.

source: Oaksford & Chater (1994) A rational analysis of the selection task as optimal data selection, as described in Coenen et al. 2019
finding: Recast Wason's four-card task as choosing a query by EIG, assuming the named properties (vowel, even number) are rare. Under rarity, testing '2' (q) has higher EIG than testing '7' (not-q), matching the common human choice that looked like confirmation bias.
numbers: Review states EIG(2) > EIG(7) under the rarity assumption. The original paper was not opened, so exact EIG values are not recorded.
limits: Secondary account only (source paywalled). Critics cited in the review (Klayman & Ha; Wason 2-4-6) favour a positive test strategy; the rarity prior is an added assumption.
agent_relevance: An apparent bias can be rational once the prior is stated. A check that flags 'confirmation bias' should compare with EIG under the real prior.

source: Steyvers, Tenenbaum, Wagenmakers & Blum (2003) causal network interventions, as described in Coenen et al. 2019
finding: Participants watched a network of mind-reading aliens, then chose which alien to intervene on; EIG over candidate causal structures predicted their choices.
numbers: No numbers given in the review.
limits: Secondary account only.
agent_relevance: Structure-learning probes can be chosen by EIG over a small set of candidate structures.

source: Coenen, Rehder & Gureckis (2015) strategies to intervene on causal systems, as described in Coenen et al. 2019
finding: Adults chose interventions on 3-variable causal systems to tell two candidate structures apart. A hierarchical Bayesian model fit a weight between EIG (1) and a positive-testing heuristic (0). Baseline: a mixture. After extra problems that punish positive testing, people used EIG more. Under time pressure, behaviour moved toward positive testing.
numbers: Three time-pressure experiments shifted toward the heuristic; one 'EIG superior' experiment shifted toward EIG (shown as posterior distributions; no point values in the review).
limits: Positive testing cannot be written as an approximation of EIG (per the authors). A link-comparison heuristic sometimes mimics EIG.
agent_relevance: Even humans use EIG only when it pays and time allows. Code can run EIG every time; the limit for a model is its weak likelihoods.

source: Rothe, Lake & Gureckis (2016/2018) Battleship question asking, as described in Coenen et al. 2019
finding: People asked to write questions in Battleship rarely asked anything near the maximum EIG question; the modal question was mundane. In a follow-up where they picked from a list, choices matched OED predictions.
numbers: Review gives no numbers (see Rothe 2017 and Grand 2024 for them).
limits: Generation vs recognition gap: people are good judges but poor generators of questions.
agent_relevance: Split the job: the model proposes many candidate probes, code scores them by EIG and picks.

source: Ruggeri & Lombrozo (2015) and Ruggeri, Lombrozo, Griffiths & Xu (2015), as described in Coenen et al. 2019
finding: Children about 7-8 in 20-questions / Guess Who games ask hypothesis-scanning questions ('Is it Bill?'); 9-11-year-olds and adults ask constraint-seeking questions. Match to EIG predictions grows with age. The review reports that part of young children's inefficiency comes from bad stopping rules (asking after the answer is known).
numbers: Ages: 7-8 vs 9-11 vs adults. Original papers not opened.
limits: Stopping-rule explanation is reported second-hand; no effect sizes available here.
agent_relevance: Two failures: poor question choice and not stopping. The scaffold needs an EIG pick and a code stop rule (stop when the posterior is concentrated).

source: Nelson, McKenzie, Cottrell & Sejnowski (2010) Experience matters: information acquisition optimizes probability gain (Psych Sci)
finding: Four theories of the value of a query (information gain, KL distance, probability gain, impact) usually predict the same human choice. The authors used computer optimisation to build environments where they disagree. When people learned probabilities by experience, they followed probability gain (error reduction), not information gain.
numbers: Experiment 1: 129 subjects, 113 reached criterion. Median subject viewed the higher-probability-gain feature 99% of the time (100 of 101 trials). 82-97% of subjects preferred it in each of 4 conditions (all p<.001). In conditions 1-2 every other model preferred the other feature.
limits: Experience-based learning of probabilities needed about 690-1082 trials to criterion. Not a language task.
agent_relevance: If EIG and 'chance of being right next' (probability gain) disagree, humans follow the latter. For an agent whose aim is a correct answer, probability gain may be a better probe score than entropy.

source: Nelson et al. (2010) statistics vs experience, Experiment 3 limits (same paper)
finding: With verbally described statistics (not experience), the preference dropped or flipped. Experiment 3 tested tie-breaking: when probability gain is equal, information gain or a chance of a certain result only weakly broke the tie.
numbers: Statistics-based task: only 27% and 30% preferred the higher-probability-gain feature in conditions 1 and 2 (experience task 82%); conditions 3 and 4: 65% and 58%. Experiment 3 tie condition: 12 of 22 (55%) preferred the feature with more info and a chance of certainty. Another condition: 6 of 20 (30%) preferred the possible-certainty feature.
limits: 43-45 subjects per condition in the statistics task, 28-29 in the experience task. 'Other models contribute little' is the authors' reading.
agent_relevance: Format of probabilities changes behaviour. An agent given verbal probabilities in a prompt may act like the statistics group; code should supply measured frequencies.

source: Nelson et al. (2014) Children's sequential information search is sensitive to environmental probabilities, as cited in Coenen et al. 2019
finding: Cited as showing children's sequential information search follows environmental probabilities, consistent with OED norms.
numbers: No numbers in the review; original paywalled and not opened.
limits: Secondary account.
agent_relevance: Developmental base for scoring probes with learned frequencies.

source: Rothe, Lake & Gureckis (2017) Question asking as program generation (NeurIPS)
finding: Questions are written as programs over a Battleship game state and scored by EIG plus complexity, answer-type and relevance features in a log-linear model fit to human questions. EIG is the expected drop in uncertainty over board hypotheses.
numbers: Mean Spearman rank correlation of model with human question frequency: 0.64 (full), 0.65 (information-agnostic), 0.55 (type-agnostic), -0.36 (complexity-agnostic). Full model beat complexity-agnostic in 100% of bootstrap samples, information-agnostic in 81%, type-agnostic in 88%. About 15% of human questions per context are novel.
quote: there is, surprisingly, no correlation at all between question generation frequency and EIG alone
limits: Human data are sparse (many questions asked once). EIG alone had no correlation with how often questions were generated; complexity mattered more.
agent_relevance: Raw EIG maximisation favours long, complex questions; the scaffold needs a length or complexity penalty alongside EIG.

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas & Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS sink ships: asking questions in Battleship with language-informed program sampling (CogSci)
finding: Language-informed program sampling: an LLM writes k candidate questions, translates each to a program, code computes EIG, the best is asked. EIG(x)=H(s)-sum p(y|x)H(s|x,y), in bits. Humans: 18 Battleship boards.
numbers: Human mean EIG 1.27 bits, best human 3.61; 97% of human questions had EIG>0. Raw LLM samples (k=1) averaged EIG 0.65-0.66 (CodeLlama-7b, GPT-4). Grammar-sampled questions averaged 0.36. With k=5 both LLMs approached the human mean; at k=10 both beat it (p<.001 CodeLlama, p=.01 GPT-4 textual few-shot). Valid program rate 75% CodeLlama, 88% GPT-4.
limits: Still below the top 10-20% of human questions. GPT-4V with images gave no gain over text-only baselines (grounding failure). One game, small closed hypothesis space.
agent_relevance: Most direct template for our code: sample k questions, let code compute EIG over an enumerated hypothesis set, ask the max. k of 5-10 already matches or beats humans.

source: Piriyakulkij, Kuleshov & Ellis (2023/2024) Active preference inference using language models and probabilistic reasoning
finding: Samples 8 yes/no questions from the LLM, scores each by expected entropy reduction using an LLM-defined probabilistic model over 10 products, asks the best. Compared with a vanilla GPT-4 questioner and ReAct (thinking about the best question).
numbers: 150 WebShop tasks of 10 items. The entropy-reduction LLM beats both baselines once more than one question is asked; after 3 questions it beats both baselines after 4. Information gain per question is higher for the first 3 questions; at question 4 vanilla gets more but little is left. Exact accuracies appear only in figures, not text.
limits: Simulated user is GPT-4; yes/no questions only; tiny hypothesis set (10 items).
agent_relevance: Gains come in the first 2-3 questions, where the hypothesis set is still wide; later EIG calls add little. A stop rule matters.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning enhances information seeking in LLMs (NeurIPS)
finding: Simulates future question-answer branches, computes an information-gain reward from the possibility set, propagates it, and picks the question with the highest expected reward. Tested on 20 Questions, medical diagnosis (DX, MedDG) and troubleshooting (FloDial): 5 datasets, 5 LLMs.
numbers: Mean success +38.1% vs direct prompting over 5 datasets and 5 LLMs; +46.6% for Llama3-70B. Over CoT-SC +33.8%, Reflexion +29.9%, Original-ToT +28.3%, Adapted-ToT +12.4%. GPT-4: DX 97.0% success, MedDG 88.0% (Gemini-1.5-Pro 81.4%), FloDial 43.7% -> 67.3%. Mean conversation length in successes on DX 2.0 vs 3.5 and 3.0 for direct methods. Llama3-70B closed-set Common: DP 51.4% vs UoT 55.9%.
limits: GPT-4 is the answerer (checked on a 10% sample). Closed possibility set in the main results; the open set is weaker (Llama3-70B open set Common: 34.2 vs 36.9). Simulation depth limited to 3 for cost. The 38.1% average is relative to a low direct-prompting base on some sets.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that an explicit EIG-style reward on a hypothesis set beats plain prompting and CoT/ToT for question asking; gains are largest on closed sets and shrink on open sets.

source: Choudhury, Williamson, Golinski, Miao, Bickford Smith, Kirchhof, Zhang & Rainforth (2026) BED-LLM: intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design (ICLR 2026)
finding: Picks questions by EIG using a belief state of LLM-sampled hypotheses filtered for consistency with the history, and a static LLM likelihood. Ablations isolate parts: marginal entropy only, data estimation, in-context beliefs, implicit maximisation.
numbers: 20 Questions, 6 LLMs (standard errors about 2-5 points). Animals, GPT-4o-mini: Prompt-Only 44%, Split 78%, CoT 55%, BED-LLM 88%, Entropy-only 79%. Celebrities Mistral-Large: Prompt-Only 19%, BED-LLM 91%. Things GPT-4o: 34% vs 64%. Llama-3.1-8B Animals: 8% vs 63%. Average gain +37.4 percentage points vs direct prompting; success more than doubles in over half of setups and never drops.
limits: The LLM prior is overconfident on few hypotheses and in-context updating yields hypotheses that contradict the history, so the authors filter and keep the likelihood static. Updating the likelihood with history did slightly worse (Animals GPT-4o-mini 88 vs 85, within error). Gaps shrink on the harder Things sets.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent evidence that the EIG step should sit in code over a filtered hypothesis set, and that the choice of entropy-only vs true EIG matters.

source: BED-LLM ablation: why entropy alone is not EIG (same paper)
finding: A question with high answer entropy but noisy answers even given the true item has high marginal entropy and equal conditional entropy, so its EIG is near zero. Entropy-only ranking wastes turns on such questions. The Entropy ablation scored below full EIG.
numbers: Animals: GPT-4o 88% (Entropy) vs 93% (BED-LLM); Mistral-Large 83% vs 95%. Celebrities: Mistral-Large 68% vs 91%; GPT-4o-mini 55% vs 72%.
limits: The Entropy ablation is still far above Prompt-Only (Animals GPT-4o 88 vs 45), so most of the gain comes from sampling and scoring at all.
agent_relevance: Use true EIG (marginal minus expected conditional entropy), not just 'most uncertain answer'. The cheap version keeps most of the gain but loses the last 5-20 points.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu & van der Schaar (2025) Active task disambiguation with LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Frames clarifying questions as Bayesian experimental design: sample candidate solutions and pick the question that best splits them (EIG-uniform), vs reasoning only in question space (implicit, implicit-ToT) or weighting by LLM logprobs (EIG-logprobs). Tested on 20 Questions and code (HumanEval, APPS).
numbers: 20 Questions: ranks of the true animal over 15 animals x 5 run seeds x 25 evaluation seeds. Code: after eliciting 4 requirements, EIG strategies gave higher accuracy of 20 sampled solutions. GPT-4o-mini zero-shot accuracy: APPS 35% vs HumanEval 70%. Rank table for GPT-4o-mini turn 10: EIG-uniform 6.8, EIG-logprobs 6.0, implicit-ToT 6.6, implicit 5.5.
limits: EIG-logprobs underperforms EIG-uniform because the LLM's own distribution is biased. The gap between EIG and implicit narrows for the stronger model (GPT-4o-mini vs GPT-3.5-turbo). More LLM calls are needed.
agent_relevance: Sample solutions explicitly and score splits. The gap narrows as the base model improves, so test that the EIG step still pays on our model (G7).

source: Zhang, Lu & Jaitly (2024) Probing the multi-turn planning capabilities of LLMs via 20 Question Games (ACL)
finding: Benchmark of LLMs guessing a hidden entity in 20 yes/no turns; also behaviour cloning and RL to improve small models. Shows unaided LLM question asking is weak.
numbers: Things / Celebrities success: GPT-4 0.31 / 0.50, GPT-3.5 0.28 / 0.27, Claude-2 0.21 / 0.31, Vicuna-7B 0.09 / 0.06, Mistral-7B 0.13 / 0.22; mean turns 17.3-19.6 of 20. RL on Vicuna 13B reached 0.27 on Things. 30 items x 5 runs.
limits: The judge is a model; Things answers are 'Dunno' about 20% of the time. The abstract says strong LLMs beat human players by a large margin (human numbers not recorded here).
agent_relevance: Unaided success is about a third at best, which is the baseline an EIG selector must beat.

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni & Bernardi (2024) Learning to ask informative questions: enhancing LLMs with preference optimization and expected information gain (EMNLP Findings)
finding: Samples multiple questions from Llama-2-chat-7B per game, builds pairs of low-EIG and high-EIG questions, trains with DPO. EIG is the training signal, not used at run time.
numbers: Candidate set of 8. Success in first dialogue / avg questions / avg EIG, zero-shot -> DPO: INLG 56.7% / 7.1 / 0.34 -> 68.9% / 5.2 / 0.45; Things 51.1% / 7.5 / 0.29 -> 61.1% / 5.2 / 0.40; Celebrities 71.1% / 7.6 / 0.35 -> 72.2% / 5.1 / 0.47. Plain fine-tuning lowered success (INLG 46.6%). With 16 and 29 candidates DPO still gained +6.7 and +13.8 points; BigBench average EIG slightly lower than zero-shot.
limits: Training-based, so outside our no-training scaffold. Only polar questions, closed candidate sets, a 7B model.
agent_relevance: EIG labels are a usable reward, and training on sets of 8 transfers to 16 and 29 candidates.

source: Andukuri, Franken, Gerstenberg & Goodman (2024) STaR-GATE: teaching language models to ask clarifying questions
finding: Self-improvement loop: keep questioner conversations that raise the probability of a gold response, finetune, repeat. A likelihood-based proxy of informativeness, not EIG itself.
numbers: 25,500 persona-task prompts; after two iterations the model's responses were preferred over the initial model on 72% of tasks.
limits: Finetuning, simulated personas, proxy reward. Not a direct test of EIG.
agent_relevance: A question's reward can be the change in probability of a verified good output, which code can compute without an opinion judge (G5, G10).

source: Li, Tamkin, Goodman & Andreas (2023) Eliciting human preferences with language models (GATE)
finding: Models elicit preferences through free-form questions or generated edge cases. Pre-registered human experiments in email validation, content recommendation, moral reasoning. Questions are prompted, not chosen by EIG.
numbers: 388 participants. GATE beat no elicitation in all domains (significant at .05 except email, where only generative active learning was). Better than user-written prompts in 6/10 settings on absolute score and 7/10 on AUC. Generative yes/no questions beat prompts in every setting. Average answer entropy across people 0.77 bits.
limits: Not an EIG selector; significance is missing in moral reasoning (low power).
agent_relevance: Prompted question asking already beats no asking, so EIG scoring must be compared against it, not against zero.

source: Handa, Gal & Pavlick (2024) Bayesian preference elicitation with language models (OPEN)
finding: OPEN: Bayesian optimal experimental design over an LM-extracted feature space picks the most informative pair of options, then an LM turns the abstract query into a natural question. User studies in content recommendation.
numbers: Metric: time-integrated delta accuracy (TIDA). Authors report OPEN beats LM-only and BOED-only methods; exact values are only in figures and were not recorded.
limits: Needs a feature space. LM-only open-ended questions did well as questions but could not use OPEN predictions. Some participants found pairwise questions confusing.
agent_relevance: A fixed feature space plus language rendering is a workable pattern for human-facing probes.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le & Ellis (2024) Doing experiments and revising rules with natural language and probabilistic reasoning (NeurIPS)
finding: An LLM proposes natural-language rule hypotheses, sequential Monte Carlo reweights them, and experiments are picked by information gain. Compared with human Zendo data from Bramley et al.
numbers: Human accuracy 5.26/8 test scenes; ReAct-style LLM 4.60; strongest model (online, hard rules) 6.55; online fuzzy rules 5.35. R2 with human accuracy by rule: 0.57 (fuzzy online), 0.10 (hard), 0.05 (batch), 0.25 (ReAct). Log-likelihood of human data: online fuzzy -1478.82, previous best model -1539, batch hard -2921.00, online hard -5209.93.
limits: Hard rules score best on accuracy but fit human data worst. Zendo and ActiveACRE are small toy domains.
agent_relevance: Online belief update plus information-gain experiments beats a plain LLM agent at rule discovery; keeping a probabilistic (not all-or-none) rule belief tracks people better.

source: Zhang & Choi (2023) Clarify when necessary: resolving ambiguity through interaction with LMs
finding: Splits clarification into when to ask, what to ask, and how to answer. INTENT-SIM estimates entropy over user intents to decide when a clarifying question is worth it.
numbers: Abstract: when allowed to clarify on only 10% of examples, the system doubles the performance gain over picking examples at random; works across QA, translation and NLI.
limits: Only the abstract claim and a few table rows were read; some table entries differ by little (e.g. GPT-3 MT at b=10%: 77.3 vs 76.1 likelihood).
agent_relevance: Entropy over intents is a code-checkable trigger for asking; supports gating probes on uncertainty (G1) rather than a schedule.
